finding_assessment.overall_assessment: The evidence establishes a very large burst of minimal TCP flow records directed to destination port 21, but it does not establish FTP application sessions, authentication attempts, password guessing, successful or failed logins, file transfer, command and control, or reconnaissance. The FTP-BruteForce label is contextual only and cannot validate those behaviors. Of the supplied candidates, only T1071.002 is plausible due to the conventional port association, and even that remains unconfirmed and lacks evidence of command-and-control use.

finding_assessment.overall_assessment: The telemetry establishes a very large concentration of short, bidirectional TCP flows to destination port 22 over approximately 91 minutes. This is anomalous relative to the benign baseline and is consistent with automated interaction with a service commonly associated with SSH. Brute force and password guessing are therefore possible, but neither is confirmed because the flow data does not expose authentication requests, usernames, passwords, outcomes, or source/destination identities. The contextual SSH-Bruteforce label is not sufficient to elevate these mappings to supported.
